To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the prevalence of HIV-1 infection in children in Haiti is 2.5% and that 80% of infected children have access to antiretroviral (ARV) therapy.

antiretroviral (ARV) treatment for HIV-infected children in resource-limited settings is feasible, effective and can be provided with high quality, even with a limited number of health care workers and resources, if the health care system is well organized and if a well-functioning referral system exists.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the following questions: (a) What are the factors that influence the decision to use antiretroviral (ART) therapy in HIV-infected children in a resource-poor setting?

In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

there is no clear evidence to support the hypothesis that the use of antiretroviral drugs is associated with an increased risk of cancer, and that the use of these drugs is not likely to increase the risk of cancer in HIV-infected patients.
the evidence from these studies does not allow us to make a clear statement about the effect of antiretroviral treatment on the risk of HIV transmission.
there is a lack of evidence to support the effectiveness of any of the current antiretroviral therapies in HIV-infected children.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the antiretroviral treatment (ART) regimen is not the only factor that affects virologic suppression in HIV-1-infested children.
the HIV-1 epidemic in Haiti is characterized by a large number of infected young children and a high rate of mortality.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the current standard of care for HIV-infected children in resource-limited settings is suboptimal.
we need to be thinking about the potential impact that the pandemic is having on the health of people with HIV and the health systems in the countries where we work.
